tier_reason: gemm.csv holds per-library GFLOP/s for Zynum, OpenBLAS 0.3.34 and Accelerate over 168 cases; benchmark code is public (bench/gemm_sweep.zig, bench/tools/run_gemm_sweep_isolated.py, reproduction commands in docs/performance/README.md), and source.json plus the performance guide state Zig 0.16.0, -Dcpu=baseline -Ddispatch=dynamic -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=10 OPENBLAS_DYNAMIC=0, and Apple M5 hardware.

corrections.caveats: Single host (Apple M5), measurements by the author. Zynum appears to dispatch SME/AArch64 kernels (feat_sme/feat_sme2 detected per gemm.csv.meta.json) while OpenBLAS 0.3.34 on M5 likely runs NEON kernels, which probably explains the 3.9x median sgemm gap; Accelerate (Apple's vendor BLAS) is the fairer comparator and Zynum is roughly even to slightly slower on sgemm/dgemm medians (0.93x and 0.99x of Accelerate's GFLOP/s) while ahead on cgemm (1.21x) and zgemm (1.47x) medians (derived from page data). Some shapes (e.g. m17_n2048_k257) are slower than both rivals (sgemm 107.2 vs Accelerate 429.1, OpenBLAS 203.5 GFLOP/s). The dataset is marked dirty (uncommitted working-tree sources hashed in source.json); at the time of checking, 199 of 203 manifest source hashes matched the files at HEAD, with build.zig, src/blas/runtime.zig, src/blas/core/matrix_matrix/structured_blocked.zig and src/blas/kernels/isolated/x86_64_structured_bridge.zig differing. Correctness is sampled-checked only, and the metadata reader reports a kernel_coverage_invalid_document diagnostic, so per-call kernel selection is not validated. Zynum runs its default thread policy (CPU count ceiling) while comparators are capped at 10 threads. Repo is weeks old (first commits page reaches back to 2026-08-10) with no external users. Level 2 timings include Python/ctypes overhead. Written in Zig with C (CBLAS) and Fortran ABIs, LGPL-3.0-or-later.

notes: All quoted figures re-derived from gemm.csv: sq1024 sgemm 1998.7 vs OpenBLAS 472.6 and Accelerate 1924.8, dgemm 556.5 vs 252.4 and 505.8; median Zynum/OpenBLAS 2.15x with 146/168 wins; median vs Accelerate 1.11x with 100/168 wins. License LGPL-3.0 (LICENSE plus COPYING), last commit 2026-09-23, 0 stars confirmed on github.com.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README, confirmed by search results) with its raw timing data checked in; data file times MKL dgemm against Strassen and other exact fast algorithms on Edison. Benchmark code and -O3 flags are public, but the icpc version and CPU model are not stated in the repo files read, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (median of five trials, sequential, ms): Strassen with 2 recursion levels 4836 ms vs MKL 5361 ms at N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x); 3 levels 15561 ms at N=6000 (1.16x); 1.04x at N=2000. Best exact-algorithm ratios in the file are 1.19x (<4,2,3> one level, N=1000) and 1.17x (<3,2,3> two levels, N=7500); the approximate Bini algorithm reaches 1.21x. Exact algorithms beat MKL in 329 of 756 (algorithm, N) data points. The PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README) reports better performance than MKL dgemm; the paper itself was not opened here.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Intel icpc (version not stated; Edison config loads gcc/4.8.0 module) with -O3 -std=c++11 -DNDEBUG -DBLAS_POST, sequential mode, Intel MKL from composer_xe_2013.5.192 (Makefile and make.incs/make.inc.edison)
corrections.hardware: NERSC Edison (data/README.md: 'Performance data collected on Edison'); data/all_sequential_algs/README.md says that because of Intel Turbo Boost the performance should be read relative to a 3.2 GHz processor instead of a 2.4 GHz processor; CPU model not stated in the files read
corrections.caveats: The 1.11-1.19x figures are derived from raw timing files and exclude the approximate (Bini) algorithm, which is faster still but numerically lossy; some rows in the data are noisy (for example one-level Strassen at N=1000 takes 405.8 ms vs 108.2 ms for MKL). Exact algorithms win in fewer than half of the data points, and the speedup is mainly at N of about 2000 and above. The baseline is a 2013 MKL on a 2014-era supercomputer node, so the ratio against current MKL on modern CPUs is unknown. The paper itself (arXiv 1409.2908) could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked); the paper claim is from the README citation and search results. Last commit 2021-07-06 (APA algorithms added); core code from 2014-2017.

notes: All record numbers match square.all.big exactly. The Turbo Boost note lives in data/all_sequential_algs/README.md, not data/README.md as the record said. BSD-2-Clause (Sandia), 32 stars, last commit 2021-07-06 confirmed (abandoned).

tier_reason: First-party numbers: README states 97-102% of OpenBLAS, and the bench files (benchmarks/gemm/gemm_bench_float32.nim, gemm_bench_float64.nim) record runs on an overclocked i9-9980XE with the nim command line, but the Nim version, backend C++ compiler and OpenBLAS version are not stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'It reaches 98% of OpenBLAS speed on float64 when multithreaded and 102% when single-threaded; 97% of OpenBLAS speed on float32 when multithreaded and 99% when single-threaded.' The recorded run in gemm_bench_float32.nim (1920x1920x1920, OpenMP, i9-9980XE) shows Laser 1874.1 GFLOP/s vs OpenBLAS 1732.2 GFLOP/s (about 1.08x, derived from page data) and MKL-DNN JIT AVX512 1737.3 GFLOP/s; the recorded run in gemm_bench_float64.nim (960x960x960, OpenMP) shows Laser 441.5 vs OpenBLAS 543.4 GFLOP/s by mean time (about 0.81x, derived from page data), though Laser's minimum time is lower (2.232 vs 2.910 ms) and its stddev is high (5.1 ms on a 4.0 ms mean).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: nim cpp -r -d:release -d:danger -d:openmp (from the float32 bench file); Nim version, backend C++ compiler and OpenBLAS version not stated
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i9-9980XE (Skylake-X, 18 cores) overclocked to 4.1 GHz all-core turbo, 4.0 GHz AVX, 3.5 GHz AVX-512 (bench file comments)
corrections.caveats: Essentially parity with OpenBLAS: the README's only win is 2% (float64, single thread); one recorded float32 multithreaded run shows Laser about 8% ahead of OpenBLAS, while the recorded float64 multithreaded run shows it about 19% behind by mean time. Each run uses 10 samples on one overclocked desktop CPU, with OpenBLAS version and compiler versions unstated. Written in Nim (C++ backend), not a drop-in BLAS ABI. The value is the int32/int64 GEMM and strided-matrix support. Last commit January 2024.

notes: README text matches the record. Recorded bench-file runs found and added; they disagree in direction between float32 and float64. Apache-2.0, 295 stars, last commit 2024-01-04 confirmed (stale).
